```{r data_pull, include=FALSE}
#starts working on pulling data here 
states <- c('CA', 'TX', 'NY')

#using pums data/filtering for Latinos
pumsdat <- get_pums(variables = c('AGEP', 'HISP', 'SCHL', 'PINCP', 'ST', 'PWGTP', 'HINS1', 'HINS2', 'HINS3', 'FS', 'OCCP', 'SEX', 'WKW', 'WKHP'), state = states, survey = 'acs5', year = 2022)
latinos <- pumsdat %>% filter(HISP != 1, AGEP >= 25)

#filtering variables
# PINCP > 0 restricts to workers with positive earnings; keeping zero-income
# respondents (unemployed, retired, not in labor force) creates a spike at
# log(0+1)=0, making residuals bimodal and collapsing R^2. Earnings regressions
# on PUMS data standardly restrict to positive earners.
latedu <- latinos %>%
  mutate(
    AGEP = as.numeric(AGEP),
    PINCP = as.numeric(PINCP),
    PWGTP = as.numeric(PWGTP),
    WKHP = as.numeric(WKHP)
  ) %>%
  filter(PINCP > 0) %>%   
  mutate(
    college = ifelse(SCHL >= 21, 1, 0),
    log_inc = log(PINCP),   # log() is fine now that PINCP > 0; no need for +1
    age2 = AGEP^2,
    female = ifelse(SEX == 2, 1, 0),
    # full-time: usually works 35+ hrs/week (WKHP)
    fulltime = ifelse(WKHP >= 35, 1, 0),

    priv = ifelse(HINS1 == 1, 1, 0),
    pub = ifelse(HINS2 == 1 | HINS3 == 1, 1, 0),
    receiving = ifelse(FS == 1, 1, 0),

    occ_cat = case_when(
      OCCP >= 10 & OCCP < 1000 ~ "Management",
      OCCP >= 1000 & OCCP < 2000 ~ "Business/Finance",
      OCCP >= 2000 & OCCP < 3000 ~ "STEM",
      OCCP >= 3000 & OCCP < 4000 ~ "Education/Legal",
      OCCP >= 4000 & OCCP < 5000 ~ "Healthcare",
      OCCP >= 5000 & OCCP < 7000 ~ "Service",
      OCCP >= 7000 & OCCP < 9000 ~ "Construction/Production",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),

    STATE = factor(ST)
  )
latedu$occ_cat <- factor(latedu$occ_cat)
latedu <- latedu %>% filter(!is.na(occ_cat)) %>% mutate(occ_cat = factor(occ_cat))

occ_compare <- latedu %>% group_by(college, occ_cat) %>% summarise(pop = sum(PWGTP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>% group_by(college) %>% mutate(percent = pop / sum(pop))

stedu <- latedu %>% group_by(STATE, college) %>% summarise(pop = sum(PWGTP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>% group_by(STATE) %>% mutate(percent = pop / sum(pop))

library(matrixStats)

stin <- latedu %>% group_by(STATE, college) %>% summarise(median_income = weightedMedian(PINCP, w = PWGTP, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

#ST codes: 08-CA, 48-TX, 36-NY
```

```{r regressions, include = FALSE}
#regressions 

incmdl <- lm(log_inc ~ college + AGEP + age2 + female + fulltime + STATE, data = latedu, weights = PWGTP)
#summary(incmdl) : look at college coefficient

incmdl_occ <- lm(log_inc ~ college + occ_cat + AGEP + age2 + female + fulltime + STATE,
                       data = latedu,
                       weights = PWGTP) 
  #running this and seeing if the college coefficient changes, if it does then occupation explains it
#summary(incmdl_occ)

privmdl <- glm(priv ~ college + AGEP + female + STATE, data = latedu, weights = PWGTP, family = binomial())
#summary(privmdl)
#exp(coef(privmdl))

snapmdl <- glm(receiving ~ college + AGEP + female + STATE, data = latedu, weights = PWGTP, family = binomial())
#summary(snapmdl)
#exp(coef(snapmdl))


library(nnet)
occmdl <- multinom(occ_cat ~ college + AGEP + age2 + STATE, data = latedu, weights = PWGTP)
#summary(occmdl) 
#weights 49(36 variable), initial value: 104387248.560575, iter 10 value: 89367317.882449, iter 20 value: 85152802.740061, iter 30 value: 85119113.752085, iter 40 value: 82747177.406749, final value: 82711872.201872 , converged


#residual check: helps say my model assumptions are valid
plot(incmdl, which = 1) 
#summary(inreg)$adj.r.squared

library(regclass)
VIF(incmdl)
```

```{r}
#WRITING FOR CAPSTONE 

#using PUMS data I can do the comparisons I want so I rewrote what I did with this data instead of tidycensus 
#using weighted data as it's more accurate of the whole population; PUMS pulls a sample of the data which could bias my results 
#IV: college education (either have it or do not) + DV: income, private insurance, SNAP, occupation
#Controls: age, sex, full-time work status, and state

#SAMPLE RESTRICTION NOTE:
#Analysis is restricted to Latino adults aged 25+ with positive personal income (PINCP > 0).
#Zero-income respondents (unemployed, retired, not in labor force) are excluded because:
#  1. log(0) is undefined — the +1 workaround creates an artificial spike at 0
#  2. They represent a structurally different population (non-workers), not the
#     labor market returns to education that this project studies
#  3. Mixing workers and non-workers in a single earnings regression violates
#     the linearity assumption and inflates residual variance, producing a bad
#     residual plot and a near-zero R^2

#used receiving instead of snap because snap is grouped and for regressions we run them on individual observations (receiving is an individual level variable) (this is for regression)

##NEW MODEL WRITING

#incmdl_occ
#adjusted r^2 : 0.345 so my model explains ~35% of the variation in income; solid for social science data 
#latinos with a college degree earn 2x more (2.02x) than those wihtout a college degree
#women still earn about 24% less than men controlling for age, education, and job status
#full time workers earn about 3x more than part time workers (makes sense)
#while age increases with age, the rate increases then flattens over time 


#snapmdl 
#college = -1.119, but once converted to odds ration exp(-1.119) = 0.33
#Latino adults with a college degree are approximately 67% less likely to recieve SNAP benefits compared to those without a degree, controlling for age and state

#privmdl 
#college = 0.8507 -> odds ratio: exp(0.8507) = 2.34
#Latino adults with a college degree are approximately 2.34 times more likley to have private health insurance than those without a degree, controlling for age and stae

#occmdl 
#most coefficients for college are negative meaning Latino adults with a college degree are significantlty less likely to work in occupations that require lower level skills such as construction and service jobs, compared to occupations that require higher skills

#residual plot
#dense cloud, slight funnel shape and slight downward trend
#residuals are generally centered around 0 which makes my model reasonably well specified but there's still evidence of heteroskedasticity and that means the model performs less consistently at different income levels (usually higher)

#for the income visualization i chose to use the logged data because it makes the distribution cleaner and data more balanced, makes it easier to compare groups too because without using the log one the graph looks stretched out and most of the data gets squished at the bottom so it's more difficult to see the differences between groups

```
